2.24(1)  The lawyer or firm of lawyers whose name appears on a
commencement document, pleading, affidavit or other document
filed or served in an action as acting for a party is a lawyer of
record for that party.
(2)  When there is a lawyer of record, the party for whom the
lawyer of record acts may not self-represent unless the Court
permits.
(3)  A lawyer of record remains a lawyer of record until the lawyer
ceases to be a lawyer of record under these rules.

BOOK_A.title: Lawyer of Record

BOOK_A.commentary:
A. Lawyer of Record
On the authority of the lawyer of record, see R.2.26n. Generally on solicitors, the traditional
English textbook was Cordery.⁴

The solicitor of record in King's Bench remains on the record and as address for service,
despite ﬁling of an appeal.¹
Having a solicitor of record is important, for it provides an address for service and a clear
right to notice (especially indirectly via the Law Society’s Code of Conduct). If there is a solicitor
of record, any arguments in court must be conducted by that solicitor, or by counsel retained by
that solicitor.
A lawyer in good standing elsewhere in Canada, and with appropriate insurance, may appear
in an Alberta court for a limited number of days in any 12 months. He or she must reveal to the
court that he or she is not a member of the Alberta Bar.²
An accused can ﬁre his defence lawyer at any time and for any reason, and the court cannot
restrain that. But criminal defence counsel does not have a similar right to withdraw, as the Rules
made by the various Law Societies provide. That assumes that counsel’s retainer is not a limited
one. The court also has power to restrain counsel from withdrawing for nonpayment of fees. That
follows Alberta’s and many other provinces’ decisions.³
The reasonableness of a contingency-fee agreement is not affected by the lawyer's ceasing to
act where the client had been refusing to take the lawyer's professional advice.⁴
B. Court Removal of Lawyer⁵
1. General Right to Choose Counsel
There are only 4 exceptions to a party’s right to choose his or her own solicitor:⁶
(a) a person chosen who is not on the rolls of active solicitors in Alberta or a reciprocating
province;
(b) usually there cannot be different solicitors for co-plaintiffs;⁷
(c) a solicitor who has a conﬂict of interest.⁸
The Court⁹
will prevent the use of such persons as
solicitors of record, usually by an order much like an injunction;
(d) a solicitor for one party who is likely also to be a witness at trial.¹⁰
It is doubtful that alleged misconduct by opposing counsel, especially years before, and
without objection then, is a ground to have such counsel removed.¹¹
But a right to choose or switch lawyers is not the same as a right to do so at the last minute,
still less to get an adjournment then.¹²

2. Tests for Conﬂict of Interest¹
(a) Two presently conﬂicting retainers
Loyalty to clients includes no conﬂicts of interest, commitment to the client’s cause, and
candor.²
In 2013 the Supreme Court of Canada in C. N. R. v. McKercher³
made signiﬁcant changes to
the law on disqualifying a solicitor from acting because of an existing conﬂict of interest between
two continuing retainers.⁴
This new rule probably does not apply to a situation where the two
clients have no direct conﬂicting interests, or the two topics worked on are unrelated, or in one
matter the person was not a client, only a spokesperson for some other client.⁵
If the conﬂict of interest results from existing and continued retainers by two or more clients,
then the lawyer should be removed from acting for any of those clients?⁶
If the named representative plaintiff in a class action has an individual claim or two against
the common defendant, in addition to the common issues which all the class members have, that
may well be an ongoing conﬂict of interest between him or her and the other class members,
especially as early negotiations to settle the lawsuit are common in class actions, so the court has
inherent power to force that named plaintiff which of the two claims (individual or common) he or
she retains the law ﬁrm for.⁷
There is a forbidden conﬂict if the duties and interests in acting simultaneously for two different
clients immediately and directly clash, or are inconsistent, whether or not the two lawsuits
transactions are related.⁸
But it must be actual interests clashing, not mere prosperity or success.⁹
(b) Past duty or conﬁdence still continues
There are a host of decisions¹⁰
on what constitutes such a conﬂict of interest to bar a solicitor,
but before the C. N. R. v. McKercher decision, those were the principal examples:

1. the solicitor or his or her then ﬁrm was once consulted by the opposing party,¹
either as the
party’s solicitor or potential solicitor, or the solicitor gave an expectation of conﬁdentiality,²
and the opposing party gave the solicitor some conﬁdential information³
which appears⁴
to have some connection or relevance to the present lawsuit;⁵
2. the solicitor has a present duty or interest which conﬂicts, e. g. is an ongoing ﬁduciary
of the opposing party, or simultaneously represents two clients with interests directly
adverse to each other, even if the lawyer’s two mandates are unrelated.⁶
There must be clear evidence of what information was given to the lawyer now sought to be
removed, and how it is now relevant, not mere bald assertions or conclusions.⁷
Or alternatively,
there must be a legal partnership, or clear ofﬁce-sharing of lawyers, without proper steps to

prevent information leakage.¹
No presumption of sharing information is created if there is no
solicitor-client relationship, and no relationship of conﬁdence.²
A conﬂict of evidence on whether
conﬁdences were revealed to the lawyer is critical, and needs a brief hearing with live evidence.³
For purposes of conﬂicts, it is usually assumed that a solicitor has the conﬂicts of interest
which any of the other lawyers in his or her law ﬁrm (partners or associates) would have, and what
looks to outsiders like a law ﬁrm may be treated as such.⁴
Fatal problems can come from a ﬁrm
merger, or even a solicitor who changes ﬁrms (employers).⁵
Even a change of ﬁrms by non-legal
employees can create a conﬂict and disqualify a ﬁrm.⁶
Rarely will the court intervene on the basis of disclosure of conﬁdences from a former
relationship, if the owner of the conﬁdences knows of this and does not mind, and only someone
else complains; the issue is impact on the person complaining.⁷
(c) Examples
The famous English Sussex Justices decision has to be read in light of the 3-part Supreme
Court of Canada test for bias, which requires that the neutral observer also think reasonably and
know the relevant facts.⁸
A smallish claim in bankruptcy ﬁled by a law ﬁrm on behalf of its client
(nothing being owing to the law ﬁrm) did not mean that if failure some years later by the bankrupt
was one of several counts in discipline proceedings against a physician, the law ﬁrm could not
furnish independent counsel to the discipline tribunal.⁹
A law ﬁrm cannot be disqualiﬁed from acting on a suit just because it has some minor and
peripheral involvement with one of the parties, on an unrelated matter. A litigant’s right to choose
one's counsel has some weight. And consent to the law ﬁrm’s acting on setting up some mortgages
has some weight where the issue was enforcing them.¹⁰
Conﬂicts of interest are often created by a move of a lawyer from one ﬁrm to another during
an ongoing suit on which one or both ﬁrms act.¹¹
It takes sworn evidence of effective measures to

prevent leakage of information, to rebut the presumption of a serious conﬂict because of such of
information.¹
It is odd that often neither ﬁrm detects the conﬂict before the lawyer starts work at
the new ofﬁce.²
But physical impossibility of wrong leakage of information is important rebuttal.³
Martin v. MacDonald and its presumptions that a law ﬁrm got conﬁdential information, do
not apply, nor prevent a law ﬁrm from acting against a (former) borrower, where the law ﬁrm had
acted for the lender alone, even if the borrower gave the lender (bank) conﬁdential information.
Quasi-client relations may depend upon actual facts and actual imparting of conﬁdences, not on
presumptions.⁴
A tentative meeting between a potential client and a lawyer to see whether the lawyer would
be retained, with no clear result, and differing views of the meeting, did not itself create a conﬂict
of interest for the law ﬁrm. The proposed legal work could not even be begun until other things
happened. There were neither a retainer nor instructions by the potential client, and no agreement.⁵
Merely sharing ofﬁce space does not link two lawyers for conﬂicts purposes.⁶
After all, English
barristers share chambers and Irish barristers share library tables, yet all their barristers can act
opposite each other.
A law ﬁrm is not disqualiﬁed just because a legal assistant there 5 years before worked in
another ﬁrm for a lawyer acting on the matter, where she recalled nothing about the ﬁle and had
told no one about it and her former boss was no longer a lawyer or connected with her.⁷
On merger of two law ﬁrms, see the Benning case.⁸
(d) Previous association
The rules⁹
on disqualifying solicitors for conﬂicts of interest do not fully apply where
the proposed new client of the law ﬁrm is also its former client and the opposite party now
complaining was someone formerly associated,¹⁰
e. g. , the former owner of the client company.
Then the court can weigh a number of factors, including danger of harm, expectations of
those who conﬁded in the ﬁrm, and appearances. One party cannot have the opposing lawyer
disqualiﬁed for having acted for a non-party in a related matter; it is for that non-party to
complain.¹¹
But in most cases who complains of the lawyer’s conﬂict does not matter?¹²
But a

law ﬁrm cannot act in a lawsuit against a former joint client, where it had acted for both the
parties.¹
A lawyer who has acted as counsel for a solicitor should not thereafter in the same
matter act for the solicitor’s lay client in a negligence suit against the solicitor, his former client.²
3. Exceptions to Removal for Conﬂict
The client can waive any conﬂict and allow the law ﬁrm to act.³
Only the former client affected
is relevant, and its waiver sufﬁces.⁴
A lawyer can have some shared interest with the competitor
of his client’s opponent.⁵
The opponent of an opponent is not necessarily related; there is no
conﬂict of interest if the two disputes are unrelated.⁶
Nor would there be a conﬂict where a lawyer
had advised other clients who also had disputes with the party against whom the lawyer is now
acting.⁷
Tactical motions to remove a lawyer, and delay in so applying, are a considerable problem.⁸
Delay may bar a motion to disqualify a lawyer if it would create a lot of prejudice, and the conﬂict
would work no real harm.⁹
Delay may lead to an order for removal whose effect is postponed until
certain steps are completed.¹⁰
If a request to disqualify the opposing counsel is late and seems
tactical, and his current representation is narrow and interlocutory, he may be allowed to continue
for now, with disqualiﬁcation for future substantive steps left open to decide later.¹¹
Even if a solicitor-client relationship had been established, removal of the solicitor’s whole
ﬁrm from acting for someone else may not be proper. Conﬁdential information was disclosed, but
the Law Society’s Code of Conduct lets the ﬁrm act if adequate steps are taken to ensure that
other ﬁrm members not learn the conﬁdential information, and those knowing are not involved in
any related retainer.¹²
Here the ﬁrm had taken many steps to that end, including segregation of

electronic ﬁles. The acceptance of two possible retainers for two people occurred in good faith
with use of good conﬂict systems, but close coincidental timing.
Merely having acted as an address for service or registered ofﬁce does not give a conﬂict later
barring representing an opponent.¹
But acting as agent for counsel does disqualify.²
A lawyer with a conﬂict of interest because of formerly acting for this layperson may swear an
afﬁdavit for use against that former client, if no privilege or other rule of evidence excludes the
afﬁdavit's contents.³
There is no blanket bar on a solicitor’s continuing to run a lawsuit, but now for the trustee in
bankruptcy or executor of his former client.⁴
A parent company and its subsidiary are not the same
client, and if there is no common fact between the two suits, the lawyer will be free to act.⁵
A suit by an injured person may be for him alone, though his insurer is subrogated to any
recovery; the plaintiff’s lawyer may not owe any duties to the plaintiff’s insurer which would create
a conﬂict of interest?⁶
The Workers’ Compensation Board was not allowed to require that the lawyer for the lay
plaintiff agree that the Board would be his sole client, as a condition of giving leave to bring a
subrogated claim. That was not necessary to protect the Board, and went beyond what s.22(1)
of the Workers’ Compensation Act requires.⁷
A retainer agreement of a law ﬁrm by two business
groups said that if the two groups disagreed later, the ﬁrm could continue to act for one of them.
That did not contemplate a falling out over the very project for which the ﬁrm was retained, and
an attempt by one group to eliminate the other from the project. That was too big a breach of the
duty of ongoing loyalty to an existing client.⁸
4. Procedure
Evidence is necessary to rule on a conﬂict and on possible consent to it.⁹
On reversed onus
of proof, see Part B.2 above.
A lawyer’s conﬂict is not excused by the fact that the opposing lawyer has one too.¹⁰
If one lawyer discovers a relationship between the judges and the opposing law ﬁrm, a request
by the ﬁrst lawyer to the ﬁrm to disclose enough facts to assess whether there is a conﬂict or not,
should be answered.¹¹

Where there is no statutory right to appeal, an interlocutory order removing counsel for a
conﬂict of interest does not go to jurisdiction and cannot be appealed.¹
It takes evidence to remove
a solicitor for conﬂict of interest, and the Court of Appeal cannot do that until there is an appeal,
so if leave is required, leave must ﬁrst be given.²
If counsel formerly acted for a now opposing
witness, counsel may be restrained from cross-examining that witness.³
If an application to remove opposing counsel expressly reﬂects on his integrity but fails, it may
attract a higher level of costs.⁴
But the costs situation may be very different where the alleged
conﬂict arose from acts of the parties themselves, not acts of lawyers.⁵
Where an individual counsel had a conﬂict but had changed ﬁrms, which had put in a “Chinese
wall”, though the individual had to cease to act in the new suit, the new ﬁrm could continue if it
conﬁrmed and undertook to preserve, the “Chinese wall”.⁶
Can a Crown prosecutor who lost her objectivity be removed by the court in a clear case?⁷
A law ﬁrm may be disqualiﬁed from acting if it came into possession of the opponent’s
secrets,⁸
but not if that was in good faith and narrow in scope.⁹
Nor if the party now complaining
inadvertently sent the information to the law ﬁrm.¹⁰
C. Separate Counsel for a Child
There is a discussion of when there should be independent counsel for a child in a custody
dispute, how the lawyer should be selected and paid, who should instruct him, and whether he
is simply to take instructions from the child or whether he is to speak independently. The court
struck down an appointment done at the insistence of one parent who seemed to be controlling
the situation.¹¹
D. Counsel as Witness
A lawyer ordinarily cannot act both as witness and advocate in the same suit,¹²
and the court
can remove him or her if likely to become a witness there.¹³
He or she (and the whole law ﬁrm) must

cease to act as counsel if the need to testify is realized partway through the trial or application.¹
Nor can a lawyer in a ﬁrm act if the previous conduct of the ﬁrm is in issue.²
It is worse if the
evidence will include argument and speculation, and so likely raise issues about the lawyer's
credibility.³
A lawyer employed by a law ﬁrm cannot act as counsel when a key witness in the trial
will be a senior partner in the law ﬁrm and his credibility will be at issue and actively challenged.
The law ﬁrm (if it acted) would be both witness and advocate and counsel’s duty to the court is
paramount. The senior partner could act as his own “counsel” at trial, but not for a company of
which he is not the sole owner.⁴
Disqualifying counsel as a possible witness may be proper even if he may not testify. It would
require proof that he would not testify (and maybe an undertaking that he would not).⁵
On the
other hand, at an early stage in a suit, a mere possibility that a related lawyer will be called as a
trial witness is not enough.⁶
Someone who witnesses someone else signing a document, does not have to “validate” the
contents of the document, nor certify that the person owns the property. If signing is not in dispute,
having witnessed someone’s signature does not make a lawyer a likely trial witness thereby
disqualiﬁed from acting in later litigation.⁷
An afﬁdavit limited to formalities or uncontroverted
topics does not disqualify a lawyer.⁸
While a pre-trial application is still undecided, a lawyer giving evidence for the application,
and his ﬁrm, should not be counsel, nor ﬁle documents, nor appear in court, nor cross-examine
on afﬁdavits, though they can give their client (even the representative plaintiff in a class action)
legal advice. But once the application is ﬁnally decided, they can be trial counsel.⁹
But if the legal
assistant to one of the counsel swore an afﬁdavit, she is not necessarily counsel’s alter ego,
and counsel is not necessarily the de facto witness. Some of the afﬁdavit's contents were the
assistant's own personal knowledge (apparently from her familiarity with the ﬁle), and the other
parts are not clearly information from that counsel.¹⁰
E. Miscellaneous
A potential future conﬂict of interest (here a personal interest, not another client) is not enough
to disqualify, e. g. an allegation of professional negligence without any supporting evidence.¹¹

A lawyer also owes duties to the court, the profession, and the public. The duties to the public
and the court cannot be waived by the client. And members of a law ﬁrm are identiﬁed with each
other.¹
Repeating direct to the debtor defendant an offer previously made through his solicitor was
harmless and a technical breach at worst, and no ground to relieve against the defendant’s
punishment for contempt.²
Though ineffectiveness of counsel is sometimes raised on appeal, it is extremely unusual to
hear it raised before the trial judge partway through a long trial. That would require clear grounds
and evidence that the incompetence (or unethical conduct) of defence counsel could not be cured
in any manner without a mistrial. Counsel are presumed to be competent. Switching counsel in
mid-stream is not a ground for totally rebuilding one’s defence from the ground up.³
If removing one counsel may do a lot of harm to one side, and whether that should be done is
arguable, litigating that side issue may advance the suit and stop R.4.33 from running.⁴
A lawyer’s change of ﬁrm admittedly created a serious conﬂict of interest for the plaintiff’s
solicitors, so it had to be removed before the plaintiff could take important steps. Not doing
anything about the conﬂict for over 3 years was ground to dismiss the suit for non-prosecution.⁵
Even when a non-lawyer might otherwise be allowed to represent a litigant, he will be barred
from doing so if he disobeys court orders and otherwise badly misbehaves.⁶
